An almanac is a book — usually published once a year — that packs together a wide variety of useful facts, data, and predictions all in one place. Think of it as a yearly reference handbook that you consult to look things up, rather than read from start to finish like a novel.

The whole point of an almanac is convenience: instead of hunting through dozens of separate sources, you open one book and find calendars, astronomical data, weather forecasts, statistics, and much more, all in one place.
What Does an Almanac Actually Contain?

This varies depending on the type of almanac, but a typical almanac includes some or all of the following:

  • A calendar — every day of the year, organized by month
  • Astronomical information — sunrise and sunset times, moon phases (new moon, full moon, etc.), eclipses, and the positions of stars and planets
  • Weather forecasts — predictions about the weather for the coming year, often broken down by region and season
  • Tidal data — times of high tide and low tide for the year, useful for sailors and fishermen
  • Agricultural guidance — the best dates to plant and harvest crops, based on the moon, seasons, and weather predictions
  • Statistics and facts — population figures, election results, records (like the tallest mountain or the most rainfall), economic data
  • Historical records — notable events, lists of world leaders, award winners, sports champions, and similar facts
  • Miscellaneous information — recipes, tips, trivia, puzzles, and other odds and ends

Not every almanac has all of this — the exact contents depend on its purpose and audience.
The Key Characteristic: It Is Annual

The single most important thing that defines an almanac is that it is tied to a specific year. A new edition is published every year. The 2026 almanac contains data for 2026 — this year's sunrise times, this year's moon phases, predictions for this year's weather. Next year, a new edition comes out with updated data.

This is what separates an almanac from a general encyclopedia (which is not tied to one year) or a calendar (which only shows dates, without all the extra information).

Almanacs come in two broad flavors:

1. General almanacs
These are broad reference books covering many different topics — geography, history, science, politics, culture, sports, and more. They are meant for the general public and contain a little bit of everything. A good example is The World Almanac and Book of Facts, which has been published annually in the United States since 1868 and is packed with statistics, records, and facts about the world.

2. Specialized almanacs
These focus on one specific subject or audience. Examples include:

  • The Old Farmer's Almanac — one of the most famous almanacs in the world (published since 1792), aimed at farmers and gardeners, with weather predictions, planting calendars, and agricultural tips.
  • The Nautical Almanac — used by sailors and navigators, containing precise astronomical data needed to determine a ship's position at sea.
  • Sports almanacs — containing statistics, records, and results from a particular sport or sports season.
  • Political almanacs — covering election results, government data, voting records, and legislative information.

• The Old Farmer's Almanac (USA, 1792–present): Famous for its long-range weather predictions, gardening calendars, and homespun wisdom. It is one of the oldest continuously published periodicals in North America.
  • Poor Richard's Almanack: Published by Benjamin Franklin from 1732 to 1758, it was famous for its witty sayings and proverbs, many of which are still quoted today (like "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise").
  • Whitaker's Almanack (UK, 1868–present): A comprehensive British reference book covering government, economics, and world affairs.
  • The World Almanac and Book of Facts (USA, 1868–present): A general reference almanac with thousands of facts and statistics across virtually every topic.
How Is an Almanac Different From Similar Things?

It helps to understand what an almanac is not:

  • Not a dictionary — A dictionary defines words. An almanac does not.
  • Not an encyclopedia — An encyclopedia explains topics in depth and does not need to be updated every year. An almanac is shallower but much broader, and is updated annually.
  • Not a calendar — A calendar only tells you the dates. An almanac includes a calendar plus mountains of other information.
  • Not a yearbook — A yearbook looks back at events of the past year (like a school yearbook or a sports yearbook). An almanac often looks forward, providing predictions and data for the coming year — though some almanacs do include a review of the past year as well.
  • Not a newspaper or magazine — Those are published far more frequently (daily, weekly, or monthly) and report on current events. An almanac is published once a year and is designed to be a lasting reference, not a news source.

Here are some natural examples to show how the word is used:

  • "According to the farmer's almanac, this winter will be unusually cold in the northern regions."
  • "She looked up last year's election results in the World Almanac."
  • "The sailor checked the nautical almanac to find the exact time of moonrise."
  • "My grandfather always kept an almanac on the kitchen table and consulted it before deciding when to plant his tomatoes."

Sometimes "almanac" is used loosely and informally to describe any comprehensive collection of information about a subject — even if it is not strictly an annual publication. For example, someone might call a detailed guidebook about a city an "almanac of the city," meaning it contains a rich, organized collection of facts about that place. In this figurative sense, the word simply suggests a thorough and well-organized repository of knowledge.

An almanac is an annual reference book that brings together a wide variety of information — calendars, astronomical data, weather predictions, statistics, historical facts, and more — all in one place, published fresh every year to reflect current and upcoming data. It can be general (covering many topics) or specialized (focused on farming, navigation, sports, etc.). Its defining traits are that it is annual, factual, and reference-oriented — a book you consult, not one you read through.
